facts.text: The azure kingfisher is a very colourful bird, with a deep blue to azure back and rufous-buff underparts streaked with blue-violet.
facts.quote: It is a very colourful bird, with deep blue to azure back, a large white to buff spot on the side of the neck and throat, rufous-buff with some blue-violet streaks on the breast and flanks.

facts.text: It has red feet with only two forward toes, an unusual trait among birds.
facts.quote: The feet are red with only two forward toes.

facts.text: The white spots on its face may help ward off potential predators.
facts.quote: The lores (the region between the eye and the bill) are white and inconspicuous except in front view, where they stand out as two large white eye-like spots which may have a role in warding off potential predators.

facts.text: Usually silent, the azure kingfisher gives a high-pitched, shrill "pseet-pseet" call, often while in flight.
facts.quote: Its voice is a high-pitched, shrill "pseet-pseet", often in flight.

facts.text: It eats small fish, crustaceans, water beetles, spiders, locusts, and small frogs or tadpoles.
facts.quote: The azure kingfisher feeds on small fish, crustaceans (such as shrimps, amphipods and freshwater yabbies), water beetles, spiders, locusts, and small frogs or tadpoles.

facts.text: It is hard to spot until it suddenly darts from a perch above the water to catch prey.
facts.quote: It is often difficult to see until it quickly darts from a perch above water.

facts.text: The nest sits in a chamber at the end of a 1 m long burrow dug into an earthen creek bank.
facts.quote: The nest is in a chamber at the end of a 1 m (3 ft 3 in) long burrow in an earthen creek bank.

facts.text: In southern Australia the breeding season runs from August to February, sometimes producing two broods.
facts.quote: The breeding season of the azure kingfisher is from September to April in northern Australia and from August to February in southern Australia, sometimes with two broods.

facts.text: Although its population is decreasing, the azure kingfisher is still listed as a species of least concern thanks to its wide distribution.
facts.quote: Although the population of azure kingfishers is decreasing, their wide distribution enables classification as a species of least concern on the IUCN Red List.
